opening_message:
Ticket 1: Alyssa Rose (employee ID E026) requests write access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E026.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Analyst
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Employee is full-time Analyst. Requested write to Payroll; full-time employees can have up to write (admin only if role owns the system). Grant write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Analyst
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E026 is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors with basic training max out at read (write requires advanced training). Requested write exceeds max, so recommend read.
reason: The Security agent's note (citing the Security DB) indicates E026 is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors with basic training max out at read (write requires advanced training). The requested write exceeds the maximum, so read is granted. Although the HR note lists the employee as full-time, the security DB evidence indicates contractor status, so the more restrictive contractor policy applies.

There are two notes with conflicting information:
- HR note: role Analyst, employment type full_time, recommends write
- Security note: role Analyst, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommends read

The HR agent and Security agent have different facts about employment type. This is a conflict. HR says full_time, Security says contractor.

Access policy:
1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if the employee's role owns the system.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if they have advanced security training. Never admin.

Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist role. Analyst is not owner.

If full_time: max is write. Requested write → grant write.
If contractor with basic training: max is read. Requested write → grant read.
